opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that was one of the more surprising results for us, honestly. Going in, you might expect the more sophisticated scoring methods to win. The L2 norm approach and memorization scores both have a really nice lineage in the computer vision pruning literature. People had shown they could identify which examples are "hard" or "atypical" for a model, and that let you prune pretty aggressively.

But when we scaled this up to pretraining large language models, the simplest metric, perplexity, consistently did better. You train a reference model, score every example in the pretraining corpus by perplexity, and use that to decide what to keep.

I'd interpret it a few ways. First, a lot of the intuitions behind EL2N and memorization came from settings that are quite different from web-scale language data. In image classification you have a relatively clean, curated dataset with labels, and the hard examples are often genuinely informative. In massive web-scraped text, a lot of what looks "hard" or "memorized" is noise: boilerplate, garbled text, duplicated spam, weird formatting. Those methods can end up pointing you at exactly the data you don't want.

Second, perplexity is a pretty direct signal of how well an example fits the distribution a language model is learning. That turns out to be a useful proxy for quality in this setting. Interestingly, we found you didn't always want the lowest-perplexity examples, which are often very repetitive or trivially easy. Keeping the middle of the distribution often worked best, which says something about wanting data that's neither noise nor redundant.

Third, there's the practical side. Memorization scores and EL2N are much more expensive to compute, especially at the scale of a pretraining corpus. Perplexity is cheap, and the reference model doesn't even need to be that large. So you get a better result and a far cheaper pipeline.

The broader takeaway for me is that there's a lot of value in revisiting assumptions when you move to a new regime. Methods that work at one scale don't automatically transfer. And it's encouraging, because it suggests that being more thoughtful about data, rather than just adding more of it, gives you real gains. In some cases we trained on a fraction of the original data and still matched or beat the full-data baseline. That's a nice counterpoint to the assumption that bigger is always better.

r001.rationale: The candidate says perplexity consistently did better than L2 norm and memorization scores, but never states that it outperformed random data selection or that it was the only metric to do so.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is from our work on pruning pretraining data at scale, and honestly the result surprised us. We compared three ways of scoring examples: perplexity, which is just how surprised a reference model is by the text; the L2 norm of embeddings or representations; and memorization scores, which try to capture whether a model has essentially rote-learned a particular example. And the simple, cheap signal, perplexity, consistently came out ahead.

I think the way to interpret that is that perplexity is actually a very rich signal about data quality, even though it's computed by a model that's often much smaller than the one you're training. It captures something about how typical or well-formed an example is relative to the distribution. When you prune using it, especially when you keep the middle of the distribution and throw out both the very low-perplexity stuff, which tends to be boilerplate and repeated text, and the very high-perplexity stuff, which is often noise or corrupted data, you can remove a large fraction of your corpus and get downstream performance that's as good or better than training on everything.

The L2 norm and memorization-based metrics, by contrast, were originally developed with a different purpose in mind. Memorization scores, which we spent a lot of time on in earlier work, are really about identifying what the model finds hard or atypical, and that's useful for understanding long-tail behavior and fairness. But hard for the model isn't the same thing as valuable for pretraining. A lot of high-memorization examples are just noise, and pruning around them doesn't give you the same lift. L2 norm had a similar issue. It's a reasonable proxy for how much an example gets represented, but it didn't translate cleanly into which examples you should keep.

So the broader lesson for me was twofold. One, the metric needs to match the objective. Quality signals for pruning are not the same as difficulty signals. And two, we should be more skeptical of the assumption that more data is always better. A surprisingly large portion of web-scale corpora is contributing very little, and a cheap, model-based measure like perplexity can find it. That has real implications for compute efficiency, because the cost of scoring with a small model is tiny compared to the cost of training the large one on data you didn't need.

r001.rationale: The response says perplexity “consistently came out ahead” of L2 norm and memorization, but it does not state that perplexity consistently outperformed random data selection.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate what those scores measure from what we want a pruning method to achieve. Perplexity tells you how surprising an example is to a model, but surprise isn’t necessarily the same as usefulness. A high-perplexity example could contain valuable, rare information, or it could simply be noise. And a low-perplexity example could be redundant, or it could reinforce something fundamental.

L2 norm depends on what you’re taking the norm of, and memorization scores try to capture a different property: how much learning a particular example depends on having seen it. So I wouldn’t interpret any one score as a universal ranking of data quality.

Without the specific results, I’d be cautious about declaring a winner. What matters is how well each score preserves performance at a given pruning rate—and whose performance it preserves. You can maintain an average benchmark score while disproportionately removing examples that matter for rare cases. That’s an important part of evaluating whether pruning actually worked.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that perplexity consistently outperformed random selection; it says the specific results are unavailable and avoids declaring a winner.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting takeaway is that perplexity is useful, but it’s not necessarily the best signal for deciding which data to keep. It tells you how surprising an example is to a particular model. That surprise could reflect valuable information, but it could also reflect noise or an example that’s simply too difficult to learn from.

L2 norm and memorization scores capture different aspects of how the model interacts with an example, so comparing them helps us ask whether surprise is actually a good proxy for training value. I’d be cautious about claiming one wins without specifying the pruning rate and the downstream evaluation. The real question is: when you remove data using that score, what capabilities do you retain, and which do you lose?

r001.rationale: The response discusses perplexity, L2 norm, and memorization scores, but does not state that perplexity alone consistently outperformed random data selection.
